## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.101850.3.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.101850.3.sa1)

This paper investigates the dynamics of excitatory synaptic weights under a calcium-based plasticity rule, in long (up to 10 minutes) simulations of a 211,000-neuron biophysically detailed model of a rat cortical network.

Strengths

(1) A very detailed network model, with a large number of neurons, connections, synapses, etc., and with a huge number of biological considerations implemented in the model.

(2) A carefully developed calcium-based plasticity rule, which operates with biologically relevant variables like calcium concentration and NMDA conductances.

(3) The study itself is detailed and thorough, covering many aspects of the cellular and network anatomy and properties and investigating their relationships to plasticity.

(4) The model remains stable over long periods of simulations, with the plasticity rule maintaining reasonable synaptic weights and not pushing the network to extremes.

(5) The variety of insights the authors derive in terms of relationships between the cellular and network properties and dynamics of the synaptic weights are potentially interesting for the field.

(6) Sharing the model and the associated methods and tools is a big plus.

Weaknesses

(1) Conceptually, there seems to be a missed opportunity here in that it is not clear what the network learns to do. The authors present 10 different input patterns, the network does some plasticity, which is then analyzed, but we do not know whether the learning resulted in anything functionally significant. Did the network learn to discriminate the patterns much better than at the beginning, to capture or anticipate the timing of pattern presentation, detect similarities between patterns, etc.? This is important to understand if one wants to assess the significance of synaptic changes due to plasticity. For example, if the network did not learn much new functionally, relative to its initial state, then the observed plasticity could be considered minor and possibly insufficient. In that case, were the network to learn something substantial, one would potentially observe much more extensive plasticity, and the results of the whole study could change, possibly including the stability of the network. While this could be a whole separate study, this issue is of central importance, and it is hard to judge the value of the results when we do not know what the network learned to do, if anything.

(2) In this study, plasticity occurs only at E-to-E connections but not at others. However, it is well known that inhibitory connections in the cortex exhibit at the very least a substantial short-term plasticity. One would expect that not including these phenomena would have substantial consequences on the results.

(3) Lines 134-135: "We calibrated layer-wise spontaneous firing rates and evoked activity to brief VPM inputs matching in vivo data from Reyes-Puerta et al. (2015)."

(4) Can the authors show these results? It is an important comparison, and so it would be great to see firing rates (ideally, their distributions) for all the cell types and layers vs. experimental data, for the evoked and spontaneous conditions.

(5) That being said, the Reyes-Puerta et al. paper reports firing rates for the barrel cortex, doesn't it? Whereas here, the authors are simulating a non-barrel cortex. Is such a comparison appropriate?

(6) Comparison with STDP on pages 5-7 and Figure 2: if I got this right, the authors applied STDP to already generated spikes, that is, did not run a simulation with STDP. That seems strange. The spikes they use here were generated by the system utilizing their calcium-based plasticity rule. Obviously, the spikes would be different if STDP was utilized instead. The traces of synaptic weights would then also be different. The comparison therefore is not quite appropriate, is it?

(7) Section 2.3 and Figure 5: I am not sure this analysis adds much. The main finding is that plasticity occurs more among cells in assemblies than among all cells. But isn't that expected given what was shown in the previous figures? Specifically, the authors showed that for cells that fire more, plasticity is more prominent. Obviously, cells that fire little or not at all won't belong to any assemblies. Therefore, we expect more plasticity in assemblies.

(8) Section 2.4 and Figure 6: It is not clear that the results truly support the formulation of the section's title ("Synapse clustering contributes to the emergence of cell assemblies, and facilitates plasticity across them") and some of the text in the section. What I can see is that the effect on rho is strong for non-clustered synapses (Figure 6C and Figure S8A). In some cases, it is substantially higher than what is seen for clustered synapses. Furthermore, the wording "synapse clustering contributes to the emergence of cell assemblies" suggests some kind of causal role of clustered synapses in determining which neurons form specific cell assemblies. I do not see how the data presented supports that. Overall, it appears that the story about clustered synapses is quite complicated, with both clustered and non-clustered synapses driving changes in rho across the board.

(9) Section 2.5 and Figure 7: Can we be certain that it is the edge participation that is a particularly good predictor of synaptic changes and/or strength, as opposed to something simpler? For example, could it be the overall number of synapses, excitatory synapses, or something along these lines, that the source and/or target neurons receive, that determine the rho dynamics? And then, I do not understand the claim that edge participation allows one to "delineate potentiation from depression". The only related data I can find is in Figure 7A3, about which the authors write "this effect was stronger for potentiation than depression". But I don't see what they mean. For both depression and facilitation, the changes observed are in the range of ~12% of probability values. And even if the effect is stronger, does it mean one can "delineate" potentiation from depression better? What does it mean, to "delineate"? If it is some kind of decoding based on the edge participation, then the authors did not show that.

(10) "test novel predictions in the MICrONS (2021) dataset, which while pushing the boundaries of big data neuroscience, was so far only analyzed with single cells in focus instead of the network as a whole (Ding et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023)." That is incorrect. For example, the whole work of Ding et al. analyzes connectivity and its relation to the neuron's functional properties at the network level.

Comments on revisions:

The authors addressed all my concerns from the previous review, primarily via textual changes such as improved Discussion. Thus, most of the weaknesses raised in the original review are not eliminated - in particular, points 1, and 5-9 - but they are acknowledged and described better. This remains a useful study that should be of interest to researchers in the field.

Summary:

This paper aims at understanding the effects of plasticity in shaping dynamics and structure of cortical circuits, as well as on how that depends on aspects as network structure and dendritic processing.

Strengths:

The level of biological detail included is impressive, and the numerical simulations appear to be well executed. Additionally, they have done a commendable job in open-sourcing the model.

Weaknesses (after revision):

- As noted in my initial review, the observation that network activity remains stable without an explicit homeostatic mechanism-while acknowledged by the authors as consistent with previous findings (e.g., Higgins et al., 2014)-is not clearly framed as a replication or validation step in the current manuscript. For instance, the abstract states: "In our exploratory simulations, plasticity acted sparsely and specifically, firing rates and weight distributions remained stable without additional homeostatic mechanisms," without noting that this outcome has been previously reported, albeit in models with different levels of biological detail. Furthermore, in the general response to reviewers, the authors list this as the first item in their summary of phenomena accounted for by the model, which gives the impression that it is being presented as a primary result.

If this finding is instead meant to serve as a necessary validation that prior results continue to hold under the authors' extended modeling framework-including multicompartmental neurons, stochastic synaptic transmission, and a modified calcium-based plasticity rule-this should be made more explicit in both the abstract and main text. Unless there were specific reasons to suspect that these model extensions might disrupt previously observed stability, the conceptual contribution of this validation step remains unclear.

I would encourage the authors to revise the manuscript to clarify the role and novelty of this result in the context of existing literature and to briefly motivate why confirming this property in their model was an important step.

- While the revised manuscript includes improvements in the discussion of the generality and specificity of the findings, it still offers limited interpretability and mechanistic insight. As it stands, the simulations provide limited understanding of the underlying principles or mechanisms at play, which constrains the broader conclusions that can be drawn from the work.

- In my first review, I suggested that the comparison with the MICrONS dataset could be made more informative-specifically by showing the same quantification of Figure 7D (7B in the previous version) in a version of the model without plasticity and clarifying the interpretation of Figure 8B, where the data appears to align closely with the model before plasticity.

In their response, the authors explain that several of these features remain largely unchanged before and after plasticity. For example, they note that total gAMPA\begin{document}$g_{\text{AMPA}}$\end{document} increases with k\begin{document}$k$\end{document}-edge indegree even in the initial model configuration. I appreciate this clarification, but it highlights a conceptual point that should be more clearly addressed in the manuscript. If the aspects of the model that align with MICrONS data are already present before plasticity, then these similarities reflect properties of the initial network architecture or baseline dynamics, rather than outcomes shaped by the plasticity process itself.

If this interpretation is correct, it represents an interesting and potentially important finding. However, it is not currently articulated in the text. The manuscript places strong emphasis on the role of plasticity in shaping network structure and dynamics, yet the comparisons with MICrONS data appear to reflect features that do not depend on plasticity. Clarifying this distinction would help readers better appreciate the implications of the model-data comparison and discern which conclusions are genuinely supported by the data.

Summary:

Ecker et al. utilized a biologically realistic, large-scale cortical model of the rat's non-barrel somatosensory cortex, incorporating a calcium-dependent plasticity rule to examine how various factors influence synaptic plasticity under in vivo-like conditions. Their analysis characterized the resulting plastic changes and revealed that key factors, including the co-firing of stimulus-evoked neuronal ensembles, the spatial organization of synaptic clusters, and the overall network topology, play an important role in affecting the extent of synaptic plasticity.

Strengths:

The detailed, large-scale model employed in this study enables the evaluation of diverse factors across various levels that influence the extent of plastic changes. Specifically, it facilitates the assessment of synaptic organization at the subcellular level, network topology at the macroscopic level, and the co-activation of neuronal ensembles at the activity level. Moreover, modeling plasticity under in vivo-like conditions enhances the model's relevance to experiments.

Weaknesses:

The paper lacks mechanistic insights into the observed phenomena, particularly regarding aspects that are typically inaccessible in traditional simplified models, such as layer-specific and layer-to-layer pathway-specific plasticity changes.

results.result: The study uses a biophysically detailed cortical network model of rat non-barrel somatosensory cortex (nbS1) comprising 211,712 neurons in 2.4 mm³ of tissue with diverse excitatory cell morphologies, conductances distributed across electrical compartments, and thalamic input from VPM and POm fibers. The model is based on juvenile rats (P14-16) and represents improvements over prior models in anatomical and physiological properties, though it uses mixed data sources due to limitations in available high-quality data.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C61, C63, C64, C67-C69 provide consistent descriptions of the model architecture, input protocols, and improvements over prior work with appropriate citations. Claims C93 and C96 acknowledge limitations regarding developmental stage and data sources. The model specifications are clearly documented with references to validation figures.

results.result: The calcium-based plasticity model implements the calcium-control hypothesis where NMDA receptors serve as the molecular substrate for Hebbian coincidence detection, with depolarization-induced calcium entrance into postsynaptic dendrites driving changes in synaptic efficacy. The model makes several assumptions including 1 mM extracellular magnesium concentration representative of in vivo conditions, excludes 8% of L6 pyramidal cells that only fire bursts, makes L4 spiny stellate connections non-plastic due to non-NMDA dependent plasticity, and does not include inhibitory plasticity, neuromodulation, or several other mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C13 establish the theoretical foundation with appropriate citations to prior work. Claims C80-C81, C94, and C97 clearly document model assumptions and exclusions with justifications. The limitations are transparently acknowledged, though some assumptions (e.g., Mg²⁺ concentration) lack direct validation.

results.result: The calcium-based plasticity rule promotes network stability during 10 minutes of simulated in vivo-like activity, with excitatory firing rates remaining stable throughout the simulation. Unlike simple STDP rules that lead to exploding firing rates without homeostatic mechanisms, calcium-based rules do not necessarily destabilize networks. The model demonstrates that network scale, biorealistic connection probabilities, low in vivo-like rates, and the calcium-based plasticity model all contribute to stability, with the rule evolving over-excitable networks toward lower excitability.
results.evaluation: Claims C14, C17, C100-C102, and C60 are mutually consistent and supported by comparisons to STDP controls (C16) and theoretical literature. Figure 2C provides direct evidence of firing rate stability. The comparison to prior theoretical work (C100-C101) appropriately contextualizes the findings. The claim about homeostatic-like behavior (C60) is supported by the synchronous-to-asynchronous transition data (C104).

results.result: Control simulations demonstrate that STDP rules induce continuous changes without stabilization, and that calcium-based plasticity can convert synchronous (unstable) network activity to asynchronous activity within one minute of biological time.
results.evaluation: Claims C16 and C104 are directly supported by Figure 2E (pink line) and Figure 2F with references to supplementary figures. These control experiments strengthen the main stability findings by demonstrating both what doesn't work (STDP) and the corrective capacity of the calcium-based rule.

results.result: Plasticity acted sparsely and specifically during simulated evoked activity, with approximately 7% of synapses undergoing long-term plasticity in 10 minutes, affecting below 18% of connections across the network. Depression was more common than potentiation at both connection and synapse levels, with Layer 5 pyramidal cells contributing mostly to basal dendrite changes and Layer 6 pyramidal cells to apical changes. The mean peak AMPA conductance decreased minimally (-2 pS), and 60% of potentiation and 40% of depression crossing the unstable fixed-point occurred within the first minute.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C18, C20-C22, C25, C33, and C132 provide consistent quantitative descriptions of plasticity sparsity with specific percentages and references to figures (3A1, 3B1-B2, 3C1-C2, 3D2). The layer-specific patterns (C21) and temporal dynamics (C25) are well-documented. The summary claim C132 accurately reflects the detailed findings.

results.result: Potentiation dominated in amplitude while depression counteracted it in frequency, leading to stable firing rates without explicit homeostatic terms. Plastic changes were non-random and stimulus-specific: random Poisson spikes without spatio-temporal structure reduced plasticity by 25%, the plasticity model is not strictly Hebbian (postsynaptic firing alone could change efficacy though presynaptic release was required for most changes), layer-to-layer pathway specificity differed from random controls, and there was strong overexpression of simplices in the subgraph of changing connections with maximal simplex dimension exceeding chance by two.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C26, C28-C31 demonstrate non-random, structured plasticity through multiple lines of evidence: control simulations (C26, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), comparison to random controls (C29, Figure 4A2-A3), and topological analysis (C30-C31, Figure 4B). The balance between potentiation and depression (C8) is supported by the stability results. The non-Hebbian nature (C28) is appropriately qualified with citations.

results.result: The propensity of plastic changes increased as pairwise firing rates increased, consistent with previous modeling insights.
results.evaluation: Claim C19 is directly supported by Figure 3A2 and citations to prior modeling work (Litwin-Kumar and Doiron, 2014; Graupner et al., 2016). This establishes a rate-dependence baseline that is later refined by showing that rate alone is insufficient (C39).

results.result: Functional assemblies were activated in all stimulus repetitions with 3-4 assemblies remaining active for 190±30 ms. Within assemblies, up to 13.8% of synapses depressed (vs. 5% overall) and up to 5.2% potentiated (vs. 2% overall), with synapses across assemblies undergoing more changes than within assemblies. Co-firing in a Hebbian cell assembly is a better predictor of plastic changes than just firing at high rates, with cells that fire together more than expected having three times higher chances of changing synaptic efficacy. Early assemblies are stimulus-specific while late assemblies are non-specific and participate in all assembly sequences.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C40, C110-C111 form a coherent narrative about assembly-specific plasticity supported by Figures 5B-F and rate-based controls (Figure 5G). The quantitative claim of 3x higher probability (C40) is supported by the comparison between assembly synapses and rate-matched controls. The functional distinction between early and late assemblies (C110-C111) is supported by their composition and connectivity patterns.

results.result: Clustered synapses within early and middle assemblies were unlikely to undergo plastic changes, while non-clustered within-assembly synapses were most likely to change across all assemblies. However, clustered within-assembly synapses that did change depressed to a significantly smaller degree than other categories. Cross-assembly synapses that were spatially clustered were likely initiated as fully depressed and had high chances of potentiation. These stable early assemblies can function as a stable backbone amid ongoing plasticity, with synapses between assemblies more likely to change, especially if clustered on postsynaptic dendrites.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C44, C113-C114 describe complex interactions between spatial clustering and assembly membership supported by Figures 6C-D and supplementary figures with statistical tests (two-way ANOVA). The contrasting patterns for within- vs. cross-assembly clustered synapses (C41-C44) are well-documented. The interpretive claims about stable backbones (C113) and enhanced cross-assembly plasticity (C114) are reasonable inferences from the data.

results.result: Network-level metrics predict plasticity: the indegree of pre- and postsynaptic neurons predicts plastic changes, k-edge indegree (number of k-simplices innervating a connection) increases probability of change across dimensions, connections with highest k-edge indegree tend toward potentiation while lowest favor depression, and high k-edge indegree predicts higher connection strength in both the model and MICrONS dataset. Within assembly subgraphs, probability of changes only increased with k-edge indegree for the presented pattern or late assemblies. Simplex motifs innervating cells predict assembly membership, and pattern-indegree (number of VPM fibers from a pattern innervating a neuron) also predicts connection changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C50, C118-C120, C122 establish k-edge indegree as a novel predictor of plasticity with validation in MICrONS data (C49, Figure 7D). The comparable network properties between model and MICrONS (C119) support the validity of the comparison. The pattern-specificity within assembly subgraphs (C50) is well-documented in Figure 7E2. The connection to assembly membership (C118) provides mechanistic context.

results.result: After plasticity, firing rates decreased slightly while spike correlations remained stable, with effects more pronounced in deeper layers. The highest correlations both before and after plasticity were found in the most central edges (highest edge participation in high-dimensional simplices), a prediction verified in the MICrONS dataset. Correlations of connected neuron pairs decreased slightly following the firing rate decrease. The most central connections of the network drive correlated activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C53, C124-C125, C131 describe functional consequences of plasticity with validation in MICrONS data (C53, Figure 8B2). The relationship between edge centrality and correlations (C52) is supported by both model and experimental data. The layer-specific effects (C125) add important detail. The prediction-validation cycle (C131) strengthens confidence in the findings.

results.result: While assemblies remained fairly stable, they became more stimulus-specific and reliable: an early assembly responding to patterns B and E split into two stimulus-specific assemblies after plasticity, assembly sequences became more reliable with significant increases in Hamming similarity for most patterns, but single-cell spike time reliability slightly decreased. This demonstrates that plasticity can contribute to emergence of robust population codes with unreliable neurons, making circuit responses more distinct between stimuli (increased specificity) but less distinct for a given stimulus (increased reliability).
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C59, C134 describe a key finding about population-level coding supported by Figures 8C-E with statistical tests (Kruskal-Wallis). The assembly splitting (C54) provides concrete evidence of increased specificity. The contrast between assembly-level and single-cell reliability (C57) is particularly important and well-documented. The interpretive claims (C58-C59) are well-supported by the data and represent important computational insights.

results.result: While prior work (Markram and Tsodyks, 1996) showed redistribution of synaptic efficacy at the single connection level in vitro, this study found network-level redistribution under in vivo-like conditions that maintained spike correlations globally while enhancing stimulus-specificity and reliability of subpopulations.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C130 appropriately contextualize the findings relative to prior work with proper citations and figure references (Figure 8A-D, 8F). The distinction between connection-level and network-level redistribution is important and well-supported. The summary (C130) accurately captures the main functional outcome.

results.result: Pattern C elicited the strongest response while pattern H elicited the weakest, and patterns H and I had the most similar responses because they share 66% of VPM fibers.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C107 describe stimulus-response relationships with clear mechanistic explanation (fiber overlap) and reference to Figure 2A. These findings validate that the model responds appropriately to input structure.

results.result: The simulations required an estimated 12 million core hours and were always repeated at least three times to assess qualitative consistency of results.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C72 document computational requirements and replication practices with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1. This establishes the scale of the computational effort and addresses reproducibility.

results.result: Assembly detection used 20 ms time bins with significance determined by the 95th percentile of 100 shuffled controls. The MICrONS dataset (electron microscopic reconstruction) with 60,048 classified neurons was used for validation, with eight calcium-imaging sessions (at least 1000 neurons per session, 85% co-registered) providing functional data from 243 neurons/session on average (1817 unique neurons total). Spike time reliability was calculated using cosine similarities of mean-centered, smoothed spike times (1ms bins, 10ms Gaussian kernel).
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C84, C86-C87, C89-C92 provide detailed methodological descriptions with appropriate citations. The MICrONS dataset specifications are clearly documented. The methods are sufficiently detailed for replication and the selection criteria for imaging sessions are justified by citations to prior work.

results.result: Adding biological complexity allowed reduction in the number of explicitly modeled mechanisms. The model and detailed instructions are open-sourced. Plastic changes were largely determined by anatomical structure of synaptic connectivity and its relation to functional units (co-firing assemblies, clustered synapses, common innervation, central edges). The model is not designed to solve specific tasks but represents sensory cortex learning stimulus features in an unsupervised manner, with demonstration of stimulus-specificity and increased reliability providing crucial validation that results have implications for learning beyond just describing biophysical processes.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C99, C133, C135-C136 provide important context about modeling philosophy and interpretation. The claim about reducing explicit mechanisms (C98) is supported by the stability results without homeostatic terms. Open-sourcing (C99) supports reproducibility. The summary of determinants (C133) accurately reflects the findings. The clarifications about task-free learning (C135) and validation importance (C136) are appropriate interpretive statements.

results.result: The model is a biologically detailed, large-scale simulation of rat non-barrel somatosensory cortex comprising 211,712 neurons in 2.4 mm³ of tissue, with diverse excitatory cell morphologies, multicompartmental conductances, thalamic input patterns, and extensive computational requirements. The model includes numerous biological features but also has acknowledged limitations including data source heterogeneity and exclusion of certain plasticity mechanisms.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly praised the 'impressive level of biological detail' and 'very detailed network model' (Reviewer 1, Reviewer 2). The editor's summary states the model offers 'an impressive level of biological detail, addressing many aspects of the cellular and network anatomy and properties.' No reviewer challenged the model specifications or construction, though limitations were acknowledged by the authors and accepted by reviewers.

results.result: The calcium-based plasticity rule maintained stable excitatory firing rates throughout 10 minutes of simulation without explicit homeostatic mechanisms, with potentiation dominating in amplitude and depression counteracting in frequency. This stability contrasts with STDP rules that lead to runaway dynamics.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly questions whether this finding is novel, noting 'the observation that network activity remains stable without an explicit homeostatic mechanism...is not clearly framed as a replication or validation step' and that 'this outcome has been previously reported, albeit in models with different levels of biological detail' (citing Higgins et al., 2014). Reviewer 2 requests clarification on 'the role and novelty of this result in the context of existing literature.' While the result itself is not disputed, its significance and contribution are uncertain.

results.result: Plasticity was sparse, affecting only ~7% of synapses, with depression more common than potentiation. Changes were layer-specific (mostly L5 PC basal dendrites), rate-dependent, and stimulus-structure dependent (25% reduction with random Poisson input). Most large changes crossing the unstable fixed-point occurred within the first minute.
results.evaluation: The editor's summary states 'The evidence supporting the main conclusions is solid' and reviewers did not challenge these quantitative findings. Reviewer 1 notes the study is 'detailed and thorough, covering many aspects of the cellular and network anatomy and properties.' The specific percentages and layer-specific patterns are presented as observational findings that reviewers accepted without critique.

results.result: Plastic changes showed layer-to-layer pathway specificity differing from random controls, with strong overexpression of simplices in the subgraph of changing connections and maximal simplex dimension exceeding chance by two.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these network topology findings. The editor notes results are 'solid with results being more observational in nature,' which applies to these structural connectivity observations. No reviewer questioned the simplex analysis or pathway specificity claims.

results.result: Functional assemblies were activated across stimulus repetitions, with plasticity occurring more frequently within assemblies (up to 13.8% depression, 5.2% potentiation) compared to the whole dataset (5% depression, 2% potentiation). Synapses across assemblies underwent more changes than within assemblies. Co-firing in assemblies was a better predictor of plastic changes than firing rate alone, with cells firing together having three times higher chances of synaptic efficacy changes.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 questions whether this analysis adds substantial insight, stating 'I am not sure this analysis adds much. The main finding is that plasticity occurs more among cells in assemblies than among all cells. But isn't that expected given what was shown in the previous figures? Specifically, the authors showed that for cells that fire more, plasticity is more prominent.' This suggests the finding may be somewhat circular or expected rather than providing new mechanistic insight, though the quantitative '3x' claim was not directly challenged.

results.result: Clustered synapses within early/middle assemblies were unlikely to undergo plastic changes, while non-clustered within-assembly synapses were most likely to change across all assemblies. Clustered within-assembly synapses depressed to a significantly smaller degree than other categories. Cross-assembly synapses that were spatially clustered were likely initiated as fully depressed and had high chances of potentiation.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 challenges the interpretation, stating 'It is not clear that the results truly support the formulation of the section's title...I can see is that the effect on rho is strong for non-clustered synapses...substantially higher than what is seen for clustered synapses.' Reviewer 1 also questions the causal claim: 'the wording "synapse clustering contributes to the emergence of cell assemblies" suggests some kind of causal role...I do not see how the data presented supports that.' The data are complex and the interpretation regarding clustering's role is contested.

results.result: The indegree of pre- and postsynaptic neurons, and especially k-edge indegree (participation in higher-dimensional simplices), predicted plastic changes. As k-edge indegree increased, probability of change increased, with highest k-edge indegree connections tending toward potentiation and lowest toward depression.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 questions the specificity of this finding: 'Can we be certain that it is the edge participation that is a particularly good predictor...as opposed to something simpler? For example, could it be the overall number of synapses, excitatory synapses, or something along these lines?' Reviewer 1 also challenges the claim about 'delineating' potentiation from depression, stating 'I don't see what they mean...even if the effect is stronger, does it mean one can "delineate" potentiation from depression better?' The predictive value is questioned.

results.result: High k-edge indegree led to higher connection strength in the MICrONS dataset, as predicted by modeling insights. The most central connections (highest edge participation in simplices) had the highest correlations both before and after plasticity, a prediction verified in MICrONS data.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises a critical conceptual issue: 'If the aspects of the model that align with MICrONS data are already present before plasticity, then these similarities reflect properties of the initial network architecture or baseline dynamics, rather than outcomes shaped by the plasticity process itself.' Reviewer 2 notes the authors explained that 'total g_AMPA increases with k-edge indegree even in the initial model configuration,' suggesting these features don't depend on plasticity. This undermines the claim that plasticity predictions were validated, as the features may reflect initial architecture rather than plasticity outcomes.

results.result: The probability of changes only increased with k-edge indegree in assembly sub-graphs associated with the presented pattern or late assemblies, being strongest for pattern-associated assemblies.
results.evaluation: This pattern-specific refinement of the k-edge indegree finding was not specifically challenged by reviewers. It represents a more nuanced analysis that addresses stimulus-specificity, which reviewers generally accepted as part of the observational findings.

results.result: After plasticity, firing rates decreased slightly while spike correlations remained stable. An early assembly split into two stimulus-specific assemblies, and assembly sequences became more reliable (increased Hamming similarity) despite decreased single-cell reliability. This demonstrates network-level redistribution of synaptic efficacy that maintained global correlations while enhancing stimulus-specificity and reliability of subpopulations, contributing to robust population coding with unreliable neurons.
results.evaluation: These functional outcome findings were generally accepted by reviewers. The editor notes 'evidence supporting the main conclusions is solid.' Reviewer 1 acknowledges these results in the revision comments without challenging them. The contrast between assembly-level and single-cell reliability is a novel observation that reviewers did not dispute.

results.result: The model's principal observations are that plastic changes were sparse (7% of synapses), non-random, and stimulus-specific, with changes largely determined by anatomical structure of synaptic connectivity and its relation to functional units (co-firing assemblies, clustered synapses, neurons highly innervated by same input, central network edges).
results.evaluation: The editor's summary explicitly states 'The evidence supporting the main conclusions is solid' and all reviewers acknowledged the comprehensive nature of the findings. While reviewers raised questions about mechanistic interpretation and novelty of specific sub-findings, the overall characterization of sparse, structured plasticity was accepted.

results.result: The model is not designed to solve a specific task but represents sensory cortex learning stimulus features in an unsupervised manner. Demonstrating stimulus-specificity and increased assembly reliability validates that results have implications for learning beyond just describing biophysical processes.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 raises a fundamental concern: 'it is not clear what the network learns to do...we do not know whether the learning resulted in anything functionally significant. Did the network learn to discriminate the patterns much better than at the beginning...?' Reviewer 1 states 'this issue is of central importance, and it is hard to judge the value of the results when we do not know what the network learned to do, if anything.' While authors claim stimulus-specificity validates learning implications, Reviewer 1's concern about lack of functional task performance remains unresolved.

results.result: The STDP rule kept inducing the same magnitude of changes throughout 10 minutes instead of stabilizing, and caused the network to flip from synchronous to asynchronous firing within a minute.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 questions the appropriateness of the STDP comparison: 'if I got this right, the authors applied STDP to already generated spikes, that is, did not run a simulation with STDP...The spikes they use here were generated by the system utilizing their calcium-based plasticity rule. Obviously, the spikes would be different if STDP was utilized instead...The comparison therefore is not quite appropriate, is it?' This methodological concern undermines the validity of the STDP comparison results.

results.result: The plasticity model is not strictly Hebbian since postsynaptic firing alone could change synaptic efficacy, although presynaptic release was required for most changes.
results.evaluation: This mechanistic characterization of the plasticity rule was not challenged by reviewers. It represents a technical description of the model's behavior that is consistent with the calcium-based framework.

results.result: Adding biological complexity allowed reduction in the number of mechanisms explicitly modeled. The model and detailed instructions are open-sourced.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly praises 'Sharing the model and the associated methods and tools is a big plus.' The philosophical point about biological complexity reducing explicit mechanisms was not challenged, and open-sourcing was universally appreciated.

comparisons.comparison: Both strongly support the model architecture and biological detail claims (C1, C2, C61, C63, C64, C67-C69, C93, C96). OpenEval also includes C71-C72 (computational requirements) and C80-C81, C94, C97 (model assumptions) which peer review groups together with architecture claims. Both evaluations praise the impressive biological detail without challenging specifications.

OpenEval supports theoretical foundation and model assumptions (C11-C13, C80-C81, C94, C97). Peer review groups some of these assumptions (C80-C81, C94, C97) with the architecture claims in R1, also finding them supported. Both accept the documented limitations and justifications.

Major disagreement on novelty and significance. OpenEval supports firing rate stability claims (C14, C17, C100-C102, C60) as validated findings. Peer review rates these as UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 2 questioning whether the stability result is novel, noting it has been 'previously reported' and requesting clarification on 'the role and novelty of this result.' The result itself is not disputed, but its contribution is uncertain.

Significant disagreement on control experiments. OpenEval supports STDP control (C16) and synchronous-to-asynchronous transition (C104) as strengthening main findings. Peer review rates UNCERTAIN due to Reviewer 1's methodological concern that STDP was applied to spikes generated with calcium-based plasticity, making 'the comparison therefore not quite appropriate.' This undermines the validity of the control.

Both support plasticity sparsity findings (C18, C20-C22, C25, C33). OpenEval also includes C7 and C132 (summary claim). Peer review accepts these quantitative, observational findings without challenge, noting the study is 'detailed and thorough.' Both treat these as solid descriptive results.

OpenEval includes summary claim C132 in plasticity sparsity group. Peer review places C132-C133 in a separate result (R11) supporting overall characterization of sparse, structured plasticity. Both accept these summary statements as accurate characterizations of findings.

Both support non-random, structured plasticity claims. OpenEval supports C8, C26, C28-C31 with multiple lines of evidence. Peer review (R4) supports the network topology findings (C29-C31) without challenge. Peer review (R14) separately supports the non-Hebbian characterization (C28). Both accept the structural connectivity observations.

OpenEval groups non-Hebbian characterization (C28) with structured plasticity evidence. Peer review treats C28 separately as a technical description of the calcium-based rule, rating it SUPPORTED. Both accept this mechanistic characterization without challenge.

OpenEval supports rate-dependence baseline (C19) with figure and citations. Peer review includes C19 in broader plasticity sparsity group (R3) and supports it. Both accept this as establishing a baseline that is later refined.

Disagreement on interpretation and novelty. OpenEval supports assembly-specific plasticity claims (C35-C40, C110-C111) as coherent narrative with 3x higher probability finding. Peer review rates UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 1 questioning whether this 'adds much' since it may be 'expected given what was shown in previous figures' about firing rate. The finding may be circular rather than providing new mechanistic insight.

Significant disagreement on clustering interpretation. OpenEval supports complex interactions between spatial clustering and assembly membership (C41-C44, C113-C114). Peer review rates UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 1 challenging the interpretation, stating results don't 'truly support the formulation' and questioning the causal claim that 'synapse clustering contributes to the emergence of cell assemblies.' The data are complex and interpretation is contested.

Disagreement on predictor specificity. OpenEval supports k-edge indegree as novel predictor (C46-C50, C118-C120, C122). Peer review rates UNCERTAIN for C46-C48, with Reviewer 1 questioning whether it's 'edge participation that is a particularly good predictor...as opposed to something simpler' like overall synapse number. The specificity and interpretation of the predictor are questioned.

Critical disagreement on validation claims. OpenEval supports MICrONS validation (C49, C119-C120) as confirming plasticity predictions. Peer review rates UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 2 noting that if features 'align with MICrONS data are already present before plasticity,' they 'reflect properties of the initial network architecture...rather than outcomes shaped by the plasticity process itself.' This fundamentally undermines the validation claim.

OpenEval supports pattern-specific refinement (C50) as part of k-edge indegree findings. Peer review treats C50 separately and supports it without specific challenge, accepting it as part of observational findings addressing stimulus-specificity.

Both support functional outcome claims. OpenEval supports C51-C53, C124-C125, C131 with MICrONS validation. Peer review supports overlapping claims (C51-C52, C124-C125) plus additional functional outcomes (C54-C59, C129-C130, C134). Both accept these as solid findings, though peer review groups more functional claims together.

OpenEval supports MICrONS validation of functional consequences (C53, C131). Peer review rates these UNCERTAIN when grouped with C49, C119-C120 due to concern that similarities may reflect initial architecture rather than plasticity outcomes. The validation interpretation is contested.

Both support population-level coding findings. OpenEval supports C54-C59, C134 as key findings about increased specificity. Peer review supports these same claims (C54-C59, C134) plus additional functional outcomes (C51-C52, C124-C125, C129-C130). Both accept assembly splitting and reliability contrasts as solid evidence.

OpenEval supports contextualization claims (C129-C130) relative to prior work. Peer review includes these in broader functional outcomes group (R10) and supports them. Both accept the distinction between connection-level and network-level redistribution as well-supported.

OpenEval supports stimulus-response relationships (C106-C107) with mechanistic explanation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific claims about fiber overlap and model response to input structure.

OpenEval supports computational requirements and replication practices (C71-C72). Peer review groups these with model architecture claims in R1 and supports them. Both acknowledge the computational scale and reproducibility practices.

OpenEval supports detailed methodological descriptions (C83-C84, C86-C87, C89-C92) including MICrONS dataset specifications. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these methodological details, though methods were generally accepted.

Both support modeling philosophy and open-sourcing. OpenEval supports C98-C99 about reducing explicit mechanisms and code sharing. Peer review explicitly praises open-sourcing (C99) and accepts the philosophical point (C98) without challenge. Both view these positively.

Major disagreement on learning implications. OpenEval supports task-free learning and validation importance claims (C135-C136) as appropriate interpretive statements. Peer review rates UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 1 raising 'fundamental concern' that 'it is not clear what the network learns to do' and stating 'this issue is of central importance.' The lack of functional task performance remains unresolved.

OpenEval supports summary of determinants (C133) as part of modeling philosophy group. Peer review places C133 with C132 in overall characterization group (R11) and supports it. Both accept this summary as accurate.
